Urban environments are the fastest growing landscapes on the planet, and transmission of diseases by urban adapted mosquitoes has increased markedly over the past several decades. The EcoGRAPH group is involved in several projects focused on mapping mosquito habitats and microclimates in cities, modeling the distribution of urban disease transmission hotspots, and projecting the future changes in transmission risk resulting from urban growth and climate change. We used satellite remote sensing and *in situ* microclimate measurements to generate high-resolution maps of temperature and linked them with mechanistic transmission models to estimate the localized patterns of potential dengue transmission in the southeastern U.S. ([Wimberly et al. 2020](#mosquito-refs)).

We are currently collaborating with Courtney Murdock (Cornell University) and Mercedes Pascual (University of Chicago) to extend these approaches to map neighborhood-level patterns of urban malaria transmission by *Anopheles stephensi* in Indian cities of Ahmedabad and Gujarat. This work will extend existing temperature-trait modeling approaches to incorporate the influences of humidity on water balance in mosquitoes. We established a network of indoor and outdoor microclimate sensors located at residential homes and have characterized spatial and temporal microclimate patterns and their land cover associations ([Jamal et al. 2025](#mosquito-refs)). We conducted a survey to assess the the interrelationships between socioeconomic factors, domestic water management practices, and malaria ([Batheja et al. 2026](#mosquito-refs)). These data are currently being used to develop multifactor spatial models to predict malaria risk across both cities. We also collaborated with partners in Ethiopia to study malaria trends in urbanized settings and evaluate implications of *Anopheles stephensi* invasion for urban malaria control ([Teka et al. 2023](#mosquito-refs)).
